points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 2: Environment and ethics
points.title: The components of a food system
points.detail: Production, processing, distribution, retail, consumption and waste, and the connections between each stage.

questions.q: Name the stages of a food system and explain how a decision at one stage affects another.
answer: The stages are production, processing, distribution, retail, consumption and waste management.
A decision at one stage constrains the others, since the whole system is interdependent.
For example, a retailer imposing strict cosmetic standards on produce causes growers to discard edible food at the production stage.
That decision increases waste and grower costs without any change in what consumers actually eat.

card.title: The components of a food system
card.front: The components of a food system
back: Production, processing, distribution, retail, consumption and waste, and the connections between each stage.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 2: Environment and ethics
points.title: Primary production in Australia
points.detail: Major agricultural industries, the influence of climate, soil and water, and the pressures facing Australian primary producers.

questions.q: Explain three factors that constrain agricultural production in Australia.
answer: Water availability is the principal constraint, since much of the continent is arid and rainfall is highly variable between years.
Soil quality is generally poor and ancient, with low nutrient levels requiring fertiliser inputs to sustain yields.
Climate variability, including drought, flood and bushfire, produces large swings in output between seasons.
Distance from both domestic markets and export destinations adds transport cost and reduces the shelf life available for fresh produce.

card.title: Primary production in Australia
back: Major agricultural industries, the influence of climate, soil and water, and the pressures facing Australian primary producers.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 2: Environment and ethics
points.title: Environmental impacts of food production
points.detail: Land clearing, water use, soil degradation, emissions and biodiversity loss associated with food production.

questions.q: Explain three environmental impacts of intensive food production.
answer: Land clearing for agriculture removes habitat and releases stored carbon, contributing to biodiversity loss and emissions.
Irrigation draws heavily on rivers and groundwater, reducing environmental flows and contributing to salinity where water tables rise.
Fertiliser and effluent runoff causes eutrophication of waterways, producing algal blooms and oxygen depletion.
Livestock production generates methane, a potent greenhouse gas, and requires substantial land and feed inputs per unit of food produced.

card.title: Environmental impacts of food production
back: Land clearing, water use, soil degradation, emissions and biodiversity loss associated with food production.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 2: Environment and ethics
points.title: Food security and food sovereignty
points.detail: The four dimensions of food security, the groups most at risk in Australia, and the distinct concept of food sovereignty.

questions.q: Name the dimensions of food security and identify two groups in Australia at higher risk.
answer: Food security requires availability of sufficient food, access to it physically and financially, utilisation including safe preparation and adequate nutrition, and stability of all three over time.
Low income households are at higher risk because food is the flexible item in a budget once rent and utilities are paid.
People in remote communities face higher prices, limited range and reduced quality because of freight distance and small market size.
People experiencing homelessness and those without cooking facilities face barriers at the utilisation dimension even where food is available.

card.title: Food security and food sovereignty
back: The four dimensions of food security, the groups most at risk in Australia, and the distinct concept of food sovereignty.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 2: Environment and ethics
points.title: Food waste
points.detail: Where waste occurs across the system, its environmental and economic costs, and strategies for reducing it.

questions.q: Explain where food waste occurs across the food system and two strategies for reducing it.
answer: Waste occurs at production through cosmetic rejection and harvest losses, at processing through trimming, at retail through overstocking and date labelling, and in households through over-purchasing and spoilage.
Households account for a large share of total waste, and it carries the greatest environmental cost because all upstream inputs have already been expended.
Relaxing cosmetic standards and redistributing surplus through food rescue organisations reduces waste at the retail and production stages.
Consumer education on the difference between best before and use by dates, meal planning and correct storage reduces household waste.

card.title: Food waste
back: Where waste occurs across the system, its environmental and economic costs, and strategies for reducing it.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 2: Environment and ethics
points.title: Sustainable food systems
points.detail: Balancing environmental, economic and social sustainability, and evaluating claims such as local, organic and regenerative.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim that buying local food is always the more sustainable choice.
answer: Local food reduces transport distance, which lowers emissions from freight and supports regional economies and producers.
However, transport is usually a small share of a food's total emissions compared with production methods.
Food grown in a heated glasshouse locally can carry higher emissions than food grown in a suitable climate and shipped in bulk.
The sustainable choice therefore depends on the whole life cycle, including growing conditions, method, seasonality and transport mode, rather than distance alone.

card.title: Sustainable food systems
back: Balancing environmental, economic and social sustainability, and evaluating claims such as local, organic and regenerative.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 2: Environment and ethics
points.title: Scales of food production
points.detail: Primary production, small-scale and artisan processing, and large-scale industrial manufacturing, and the trade-offs between them.

questions.q: Compare small-scale artisan production with large-scale industrial food manufacturing.
answer: Artisan production uses manual methods and small batches, allowing variation, distinctive character and close control of ingredients.
Industrial manufacturing uses mechanised, continuous processes designed for consistency and volume.
Industrial production achieves far lower unit costs through economies of scale, which makes food cheaper and more widely available.
It sacrifices variation and flexibility, requires standardised inputs, and often relies on additives to achieve consistency and shelf life.

card.title: Scales of food production
back: Primary production, small-scale and artisan processing, and large-scale industrial manufacturing, and the trade-offs between them.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 2: Environment and ethics
points.title: Levels of food processing
points.detail: Minimally processed, processed and ultra-processed foods, the purposes of processing and the nutritional consequences.

questions.q: Distinguish between processed and ultra-processed foods and explain why the distinction matters nutritionally.
answer: Processed foods are made by adding ingredients such as salt, sugar or oil to whole foods, for example canned vegetables or cheese.

Ultra-processed foods are industrial formulations made largely from substances extracted from foods, with additives for colour, flavour and texture, and often bear little resemblance to their original ingredients.
Ultra-processed foods are typically energy dense, high in added sugar, salt and saturated fat and low in fibre and micronutrients.
They are also engineered for palatability, which encourages over-consumption, and diets high in them are associated with obesity and chronic disease.

card.title: Levels of food processing
back: Minimally processed, processed and ultra-processed foods, the purposes of processing and the nutritional consequences.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 2: Environment and ethics
points.title: Why food is processed
points.detail: Preservation, safety, convenience, palatability, nutrition and cost as reasons for processing, and the trade-offs involved.

questions.q: Explain four reasons food is processed and identify a trade-off in one of them.
answer: Preservation extends shelf life, reducing waste and allowing food to be transported and stored.
Safety processing, such as pasteurisation, destroys pathogens that would otherwise cause illness.
Convenience reduces the time and skill required to prepare a meal, which suits time-poor households.

Fortification adds nutrients such as folate or iodine at population scale; the trade-off is that many processing methods that improve shelf life and palatability also reduce fibre and micronutrients and increase salt, sugar or fat.

card.title: Why food is processed
back: Preservation, safety, convenience, palatability, nutrition and cost as reasons for processing, and the trade-offs involved.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 2: Environment and ethics
points.title: Preservation methods
points.detail: Drying, freezing, canning, fermentation, chemical preservation and modified atmosphere packaging, and the principles behind each.

questions.q: Explain the principle behind drying and freezing as preservation methods.
answer: Microbial growth requires available water, so drying removes moisture and lowers water activity below the level microorganisms need.
This inhibits bacteria, yeasts and moulds and also slows enzymic reactions, though it changes texture and can reduce heat-sensitive vitamins.
Freezing converts water to ice, which both removes available water and lowers temperature so far that microbial and enzymic activity nearly stops.
Freezing does not kill microorganisms, so they resume activity on thawing, which is why thawed food must be handled as fresh and not refrozen.

card.title: Preservation methods
back: Drying, freezing, canning, fermentation, chemical preservation and modified atmosphere packaging, and the principles behind each.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 2: Environment and ethics
points.title: Food regulation and labelling standards
points.detail: The role of food standards in setting requirements for labelling, additives, contaminants and safety across Australia and New Zealand.

questions.q: Name four items required on a packaged food label and explain the purpose of the nutrition information panel.
answer: Labels must show the name of the food, the ingredients list in descending order of weight, a date mark, and the nutrition information panel.
They must also show allergen declarations, storage directions, the country of origin and the name and address of the supplier.
The nutrition information panel gives the quantity of energy, protein, fat, saturated fat, carbohydrate, sugars and sodium per serve and per 100 grams.
The per 100 gram column is the basis for comparing products, since serving sizes differ between manufacturers and are not standardised.

card.title: Food regulation and labelling standards
back: The role of food standards in setting requirements for labelling, additives, contaminants and safety across Australia and New Zealand.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 2: Environment and ethics
points.title: Food marketing and consumer influence
points.detail: Advertising, packaging, placement, pricing and health claims as influences on food choice, and their effect on dietary patterns.

questions.q: Explain three ways food marketing influences consumer choice beyond advertising.
answer: Placement in store, including end-of-aisle displays and checkout positioning, increases purchases of items consumers did not plan to buy.
Pricing strategies such as multi-buy discounts encourage larger purchases, which increases both consumption and waste.
Packaging design and front-of-pack claims direct attention to a favourable attribute while distracting from the nutrition information panel.
A product can be truthfully labelled low fat while being high in added sugar, so a single claim can create a misleading overall impression.

card.title: Food marketing and consumer influence
back: Advertising, packaging, placement, pricing and health claims as influences on food choice, and their effect on dietary patterns.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 1: The science of food
points.title: Food spoilage
points.detail: Microbial, enzymic and chemical spoilage, the conditions that accelerate each, and the difference between spoilage and food poisoning.

questions.q: Distinguish food spoilage from food poisoning and explain why the distinction matters for safety.
answer: Spoilage is deterioration in quality caused by microorganisms, enzymes or chemical change, producing off odours, textures and flavours.
Food poisoning is illness caused by pathogenic microorganisms or their toxins in food.
The distinction matters because pathogenic organisms often produce no detectable change in appearance, smell or taste.
Food can therefore be dangerously contaminated while appearing perfectly fresh, which is why safe handling cannot rely on sensory judgement.

card.title: Food spoilage
back: Microbial, enzymic and chemical spoilage, the conditions that accelerate each, and the difference between spoilage and food poisoning.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 1: The science of food
points.title: Conditions for microbial growth
points.detail: Food, acidity, temperature, time, oxygen and moisture as requirements for bacterial growth, and the temperature danger zone.

questions.q: Name the conditions bacteria require to multiply and state the temperature danger zone and the two-hour four-hour guidance.
answer: Bacteria require a food source, suitable acidity, favourable temperature, time, appropriate oxygen conditions and available moisture.
The temperature danger zone is between 5 and 60 degrees Celsius, where bacteria multiply most rapidly.
Potentially hazardous food held in the danger zone for under two hours may be refrigerated or used immediately.
Between two and four hours it must be used immediately, and beyond four hours it must be discarded, since the cumulative time in the zone is what matters.

card.title: Conditions for microbial growth
back: Food, acidity, temperature, time, oxygen and moisture as requirements for bacterial growth, and the temperature danger zone.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 1: The science of food
points.title: Safe food handling
points.detail: Cross-contamination, personal hygiene, cleaning and sanitising, safe thawing and reheating, and the storage of high risk foods.

questions.q: Explain cross-contamination and four practices that prevent it.
answer: Cross-contamination is the transfer of pathogens from one food, surface or person to ready-to-eat food.
Use separate boards, knives and utensils for raw meat and for ready-to-eat food, or wash and sanitise between uses.
Store raw meat on the lowest shelf of the refrigerator in sealed containers so juices cannot drip onto other foods.
Wash hands thoroughly between handling raw and ready-to-eat food, and clean then sanitise surfaces, since cleaning removes soil while sanitising reduces microorganisms.

card.title: Safe food handling
back: Cross-contamination, personal hygiene, cleaning and sanitising, safe thawing and reheating, and the storage of high risk foods.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 1: The science of food
points.title: Common foodborne pathogens
points.detail: Salmonella, Campylobacter, Listeria, E. coli and Staphylococcus aureus, their typical sources and the groups most at risk.

questions.q: Name two foodborne pathogens with their typical sources, and explain why Listeria is of particular concern for some groups.
answer: Salmonella is associated with raw poultry, eggs and unwashed produce, and causes gastrointestinal illness.
Campylobacter is associated particularly with raw and undercooked poultry and unpasteurised milk.
Listeria is of particular concern because it can grow at refrigeration temperatures, unlike most pathogens.
It poses serious risk to pregnant women, the elderly, infants and immunocompromised people, which is why these groups are advised to avoid soft cheeses, pre-prepared salads and cold cured meats.

card.title: Common foodborne pathogens
back: Salmonella, Campylobacter, Listeria, E. coli and Staphylococcus aureus, their typical sources and the groups most at risk.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 1: The science of food
points.title: Food allergies and intolerances
points.detail: The distinction between an immune-mediated allergy and an intolerance, the major allergens and the requirements for allergen management.

questions.q: Distinguish a food allergy from a food intolerance and explain why allergen declaration is mandatory.
answer: A food allergy is an immune response to a protein in a food, which can cause anaphylaxis and be fatal in minutes.
A food intolerance is a non-immune adverse reaction, often digestive, which causes discomfort but is not life threatening.
Allergen declaration is mandatory because even trace amounts can trigger a severe reaction in a sensitised person.
Businesses must therefore declare the major allergens, prevent cross-contact during preparation and provide accurate information on request.

card.title: Food allergies and intolerances
back: The distinction between an immune-mediated allergy and an intolerance, the major allergens and the requirements for allergen management.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 1: The science of food
points.title: Functional properties of food components
points.detail: Gelatinisation, denaturation and coagulation, caramelisation and the Maillard reaction, emulsification, aeration and gluten development.

questions.q: Explain gelatinisation and the Maillard reaction, naming the components involved in each.
answer: Gelatinisation occurs when starch granules are heated in liquid, absorbing water and swelling until they rupture and thicken the mixture.
It requires starch, liquid, heat and agitation, and is the principle behind thickening a sauce with flour or cornflour.
The Maillard reaction occurs between amino acids in protein and reducing sugars at high temperature in a relatively dry environment.
It produces the brown colour and complex flavours of roasted meat, bread crust and toasted grains, and is distinct from caramelisation, which involves sugar alone.

card.title: Functional properties of food components
back: Gelatinisation, denaturation and coagulation, caramelisation and the Maillard reaction, emulsification, aeration and gluten development.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 1: The science of food
points.title: Sensory evaluation
points.detail: Appearance, aroma, flavour, texture and sound as sensory properties, and the use of objective testing procedures.

questions.q: Explain how a sensory evaluation should be conducted to produce reliable results.
answer: Use a defined sensory panel and identical conditions for every sample, including portion size, temperature, lighting and serving vessel.
Code samples randomly so tasters do not know which product they are assessing, preventing expectation from influencing judgement.
Provide water or plain crackers between samples to clear the palate, and randomise the order in which samples are presented.
Use a structured scale or ranking sheet with defined descriptors, so results can be compared across tasters rather than recorded as opinion.

card.title: Sensory evaluation
back: Appearance, aroma, flavour, texture and sound as sensory properties, and the use of objective testing procedures.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 1: Navigating food information
points.title: Evaluating food information sources
points.detail: Assessing the authority, evidence base, currency and commercial interest behind nutrition claims and dietary advice.

questions.q: State four questions to ask when evaluating a nutrition claim found online.
answer: Who is making the claim, and do they hold relevant qualifications such as accredited practising dietitian status?
What evidence supports it, and is that evidence from controlled research on humans rather than testimonial or animal studies?
Is there a commercial interest, such as a product being sold alongside the advice?
Is the claim consistent with current national dietary guidance, and if it contradicts it, is the contradiction explained by evidence rather than assertion?

card.title: Evaluating food information sources
back: Assessing the authority, evidence base, currency and commercial interest behind nutrition claims and dietary advice.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 1: Navigating food information
points.title: Fad diets and food trends
points.detail: The common features of fad diets, why they appeal, and their nutritional and behavioural risks.

questions.q: Identify three features common to fad diets and explain why they usually fail in the long term.
answer: They promise rapid results, exclude whole food groups and often require the purchase of specific products or supplements.
They rely on testimonial rather than evidence, and frequently claim a single food or nutrient explains weight or health.
They usually produce short-term weight loss because they restrict energy intake, which sustains their reputation.
They fail long term because severe restriction is difficult to maintain, weight returns when normal eating resumes, and excluding food groups risks nutrient deficiency.

card.title: Fad diets and food trends
back: The common features of fad diets, why they appeal, and their nutritional and behavioural risks.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 1: Navigating food information
points.title: Health claims and front-of-pack labelling
points.detail: Nutrition content claims, general and high level health claims, and interpreting front-of-pack rating systems.

questions.q: Distinguish a nutrition content claim from a health claim, and explain a limitation of front-of-pack star ratings.
answer: A nutrition content claim states the presence or level of a nutrient, such as good source of fibre or low in fat.
A health claim relates a food or nutrient to a health effect, and must be based on approved relationships supported by evidence.
Front-of-pack star ratings summarise a product's overall nutritional profile into a single figure, which makes comparison quick for consumers.

The limitation is that the algorithm compares within categories and can rate a highly processed product favourably relative to its peers, so it should be read alongside the ingredients list and nutrition information panel.

card.title: Health claims and front-of-pack labelling
back: Nutrition content claims, general and high level health claims, and interpreting front-of-pack rating systems.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 1: Navigating food information
points.title: Influences on food choice
points.detail: Sensory, psychological, social, cultural, economic and practical influences, and the interaction between them.

questions.q: Explain four categories of influence on an individual's food choices.
answer: Sensory influences include taste, aroma, texture and appearance, and are the most immediate determinant of whether a food is eaten again.
Psychological influences include mood, habit, food memories and the use of food for comfort or reward.
Social and cultural influences include family practices, religious requirements, peer expectations and the norms of the community.
Economic and practical influences include income, price, the time available to prepare food, cooking skills and physical access to shops.

card.title: Influences on food choice
back: Sensory, psychological, social, cultural, economic and practical influences, and the interaction between them.

points.area: Unit 4: Food issues, challenges and futures — AoS 1: Navigating food information
points.title: Behaviour change and food habits
points.detail: Why knowledge alone does not change behaviour, and the role of environment, skill, cost and habit in sustaining dietary change.

questions.q: Explain why nutrition education alone rarely changes eating behaviour, and what else is required.
answer: Most people already know broadly what constitutes a healthy diet, so lack of knowledge is rarely the limiting factor.
Behaviour is shaped by the surrounding environment, including what is available, affordable and convenient at the moment of choice.
Skills and time matter, since knowing what to eat does not help a person who cannot cook it or has no time to.
Sustained change therefore requires changes to the food environment, practical skills, affordability and small habitual changes rather than information alone.

card.title: Behaviour change and food habits
back: Why knowledge alone does not change behaviour, and the role of environment, skill, cost and habit in sustaining dietary change.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 1: The science of food
points.title: Macronutrients
points.detail: Carbohydrate, protein and fat: their functions, food sources, energy contribution and the effects of inadequate or excessive intake.

questions.q: State the primary function and energy value of each macronutrient.
answer: Carbohydrate is the body's preferred energy source, providing about 17 kilojoules per gram, and fibre supports digestive health.
Protein provides amino acids for growth, repair and the synthesis of enzymes and antibodies, and provides about 17 kilojoules per gram.
Fat provides about 37 kilojoules per gram, supplies essential fatty acids, carries fat-soluble vitamins and provides insulation and organ protection.
Because fat is more than twice as energy dense, high fat foods contribute disproportionately to total energy intake.

card.title: Macronutrients
back: Carbohydrate, protein and fat: their functions, food sources, energy contribution and the effects of inadequate or excessive intake.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 1: The science of food
points.title: Micronutrients
points.detail: Key vitamins and minerals including iron, calcium, folate, iodine and vitamins C and D, their functions and the consequences of deficiency.

questions.q: Explain the function of iron and calcium and the consequence of deficiency in each.
answer: Iron forms part of haemoglobin, which transports oxygen in the blood, and deficiency causes anaemia with fatigue, pallor and reduced concentration.
Iron from animal sources is absorbed more readily than plant iron, and vitamin C consumed alongside plant sources improves absorption.
Calcium is required for bone and tooth structure, muscle contraction, nerve function and blood clotting.
Inadequate calcium, particularly during adolescence when peak bone mass is established, increases the risk of osteoporosis in later life.

card.title: Micronutrients
back: Key vitamins and minerals including iron, calcium, folate, iodine and vitamins C and D, their functions and the consequences of deficiency.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 1: The science of food
points.title: Dietary guidance
points.detail: The Australian Dietary Guidelines and the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating, and how each is used.

questions.q: Distinguish the Australian Dietary Guidelines from the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating and state two guidelines.
answer: The Guidelines are written evidence-based recommendations about the types and amounts of food that promote health.
The Guide to Healthy Eating is a visual pie chart showing the proportions of the five food groups to be eaten daily.
One guideline is to enjoy a wide variety of nutritious foods from the five food groups every day.
Another is to limit intake of foods containing saturated fat, added salt, added sugars and alcohol.

card.title: Dietary guidance
back: The Australian Dietary Guidelines and the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating, and how each is used.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 2: Food choices, health and wellbeing
points.title: Diet-related conditions
points.detail: The relationship between dietary patterns and overweight, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, some cancers and dental caries.

questions.q: Explain how a diet high in ultra-processed foods contributes to type 2 diabetes.
answer: Such diets are energy dense and highly palatable, which encourages intake beyond energy requirements and leads to weight gain.
Excess body fat, particularly around the abdomen, increases insulin resistance so cells respond less effectively to insulin.
Refined carbohydrates and added sugars produce rapid rises in blood glucose, increasing the demand placed on the pancreas.
Sustained over years, the pancreas cannot maintain sufficient insulin production, and blood glucose remains elevated, which is type 2 diabetes.

card.title: Diet-related conditions
back: The relationship between dietary patterns and overweight, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, some cancers and dental caries.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 2: Food choices, health and wellbeing
points.title: Nutritional needs across the lifespan
points.detail: The differing requirements of children, adolescents, adults, older adults and pregnancy, and the reasons for those differences.

questions.q: Explain why adolescents and older adults have different nutritional priorities.
answer: Adolescents undergo rapid growth and development, so energy, protein, calcium and iron requirements are high relative to body size.
Calcium intake during adolescence determines peak bone mass, and menstruating girls require additional iron.
Older adults have lower energy requirements as muscle mass and activity decline, but their requirements for most nutrients are unchanged or higher.
Their diets therefore need to be more nutrient dense, with attention to protein for muscle maintenance, calcium and vitamin D for bone, and fibre and fluid for digestive function.

card.title: Nutritional needs across the lifespan
back: The differing requirements of children, adolescents, adults, older adults and pregnancy, and the reasons for those differences.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 2: Food choices, health and wellbeing
points.title: Recipe interpretation and mise en place
points.detail: Reading a recipe fully, preparing ingredients and equipment before commencing, and sequencing tasks efficiently.

questions.q: Explain the practice of mise en place and why it improves a practical outcome.
answer: Mise en place means preparing and measuring all ingredients and assembling equipment before cooking begins.
It prevents interruptions once cooking has started, when timing is critical and a delay can spoil the outcome.
It also reveals missing ingredients or equipment before the point at which they are needed, when substitution is still possible.

card.title: Recipe interpretation and mise en place
card.front: Recipe interpretation and mise en place
back: Reading a recipe fully, preparing ingredients and equipment before commencing, and sequencing tasks efficiently.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 2: Food choices, health and wellbeing
points.title: Preparation and cooking techniques
points.detail: Knife skills, dry and moist heat methods, and the effect of each method on texture, flavour and nutritional value.

questions.q: Compare dry and moist heat cooking methods and explain the effect of each on a tough cut of meat.
answer: Dry heat methods such as roasting, grilling and frying cook without added liquid and promote browning through the Maillard reaction.
Moist heat methods such as boiling, steaming, braising and stewing cook in liquid or steam at or below boiling point.
A tough cut is high in connective tissue, which requires long slow cooking in moisture to convert collagen to gelatine and tenderise the meat.
Dry heat applied quickly to such a cut leaves it tough, which is why braising and stewing are used for these cuts and grilling for tender ones.

card.title: Preparation and cooking techniques
back: Knife skills, dry and moist heat methods, and the effect of each method on texture, flavour and nutritional value.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 2: Food choices, health and wellbeing
points.title: Recipe modification
points.detail: Adapting recipes for nutritional improvement, dietary requirements, cost or available ingredients, and predicting the effect on the outcome.

questions.q: Explain how you would modify a recipe to reduce saturated fat and what effect this may have on the product.
answer: Substitute a mono or polyunsaturated oil for butter, or reduce the quantity of fat and replace part of it with a moist ingredient such as fruit puree.
Choose lean meat, trim visible fat and use reduced fat dairy where the recipe allows it.
Fat contributes tenderness, moisture, flavour and aeration, so reducing it can produce a drier, tougher or less flavoursome result.
The modification must therefore be tested and balanced, since a nutritionally improved product that is unpalatable will not be eaten.

card.title: Recipe modification
back: Adapting recipes for nutritional improvement, dietary requirements, cost or available ingredients, and predicting the effect on the outcome.

points.area: Unit 3: Food in daily life — AoS 2: Food choices, health and wellbeing
points.title: Evaluating a food product
points.detail: Assessing a practical outcome against sensory properties, the original intention and any dietary or cost requirements.

questions.q: Explain how to evaluate a food product you have prepared.
answer: Assess each sensory property separately: appearance, aroma, flavour, texture and where relevant sound.
Compare the outcome against the intended result and against any criteria set, such as a nutritional target or cost limit.
Identify the specific cause of any shortcoming, linking it to a preparation or cooking decision rather than describing the fault alone.
State what you would change in the process next time, which demonstrates understanding of the underlying food science.

card.title: Evaluating a food product
back: Assessing a practical outcome against sensory properties, the original intention and any dietary or cost requirements.

points.area: Exam technique
points.title: Command terms and mark allocation
points.detail: Matching the depth of the response to the command term and the marks available, and addressing every part of a question.

questions.q: Explain how 'describe', 'explain' and 'evaluate' differ in Food Studies responses.
answer: Describe requires an account of the features or process, stating what happens without giving reasons.
Explain requires the reasons or mechanism, showing how or why the outcome occurs, often referring to food science.
Evaluate requires weighing advantages against disadvantages and reaching a stated judgement, which must be explicit to earn full marks.

card.title: Command terms and mark allocation
back: Matching the depth of the response to the command term and the marks available, and addressing every part of a question.

points.area: Exam technique
points.title: Using food science terminology
points.detail: Naming reactions, properties and processes precisely rather than describing them in everyday language.

questions.q: Give three pairs of commonly confused Food Studies terms and distinguish each.
answer: Caramelisation involves sugar alone browning under heat, while the Maillard reaction requires both protein and reducing sugars.
Denaturation is the unfolding of a protein's structure, while coagulation is the subsequent setting as unfolded proteins bond together.
Cleaning removes visible soil and food residue, while sanitising reduces microorganisms to a safe level, and both are required.

card.title: Using food science terminology
back: Naming reactions, properties and processes precisely rather than describing them in everyday language.

points.area: Exam technique
points.title: Applying knowledge to a scenario
points.detail: Using the specific details of the scenario given, including the people, setting and constraints described, rather than answering generically.

questions.q: Explain why a generic answer scores poorly on a Food Studies scenario question.
answer: Marks are awarded for applying knowledge to the particular circumstances described, such as the household's budget, time, skills or dietary needs.
A generic answer about healthy eating demonstrates recall but not the judgement the question is testing.
Strong responses refer directly to details from the scenario and explain why the recommendation suits those specific constraints.

card.title: Applying knowledge to a scenario
back: Using the specific details of the scenario given, including the people, setting and constraints described, rather than answering generically.
